assessment.nobel_worthiness: Strong coherent coupling of a single superconducting artificial atom to a single microwave photon in a resonator opened a new regime of light-matter interaction on a chip. It gave the dispersive readout, photon-number-resolved control and two-qubit entanglement protocols that underpin virtually all superconducting quantum processors. It is a clean case of foundational quantum optics becoming an enabling platform, and a natural successor to the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits.
assessment.attribution: The 2004 theory proposal (Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin, Schoelkopf) and the Wallraff et al. strong-coupling experiment are the decisive pair, with Schoelkopf's Yale group driving the follow-on circuit-QED toolbox. Four credited names exceed the three-person limit; Girvin has a strong claim as a theory originator, and Blais as lead theorist, so excluding one is a real judgement call. I propose theory plus the two experimental leaders.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced and extended in many laboratories over two decades, including at Chalmers, ETH, Yale and elsewhere. Interpretation is stable and the technology is mature. Timing is good, though a committee may feel the 2025 prize recently covered adjacent ground.
uncertainties: Who among Girvin, Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf is dropped to fit three laureates.
Overlap in the public mind with the 2025 prize may be seen as too close or as a natural follow-up.
I am close to this community, so my own expertise may bias my weighting; I flag the conflict-of-interest concern.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for quantum gates with laser-cooled trapped ions, and its experimental realisation with high-fidelity gates, entanglement of many ions and digital quantum simulation, established the first fully controllable multi-qubit quantum platform. It is original, clear and has had lasting impact on quantum information science and precision physics.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller made the 1995 theory proposal; Blatt (with Wineland's earlier recognised work and other groups such as Innsbruck and NIST) delivered decisive experimental demonstrations. The trio is a coherent configuration, although Wineland was already honoured in 2012 and other experimentalists such as Monroe or Wineland-group members could claim credit.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed independently by many groups over thirty years, with commercial machines in operation. Recognition is timely or somewhat overdue relative to the field's impact.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize to Haroche and Wineland may be raised.
Allocation of experimental credit between Blatt, Monroe and others is unresolved.
Zoller also appears on other candidate lines, which affects how prize slots are shared.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum error correction, the threshold theorem and topological codes show that quantum information can in principle be protected against noise, which makes large-scale quantum computing conceptually possible. The ideas are original and deeply influential, and experiments with surface codes are now crossing break-even thresholds.
assessment.attribution: Shor's code and fault-tolerance ideas, Steane's independent code construction and Kitaev's topological codes are separate decisive steps; Calderbank, Gottesman, Knill, Laflamme and others also contributed and are not credited here, so the three-person list leaves out real contributors. Shor's factoring algorithm is a distinct discovery.
assessment.maturity: Experimental demonstrations of logical-qubit improvement are recent and still developing, so the physical impact is partly prospective. The theory itself is long settled. As a theorist I value it, but I would ask whether a Physics prize fits mathematical and information-theoretic results.
uncertainties: Whether this is physics or computer science for prize purposes.
Credit allocation among Shor, Steane, Kitaev, Calderbank, Gottesman and others.
Experimental validation of fault tolerance is still early.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantized conductance in ballistic point contacts, observed in 1988 by Delft/Philips and Cambridge groups, was a clean demonstration that electrical conduction in nanostructures is controlled by quantum modes. It founded modern mesoscopic transport, and quantum point contacts are now standard building blocks in quantum-dot qubits and electron interferometers. This resonates with my own training in mesoscopic transport.
assessment.attribution: Two groups reported the effect almost simultaneously: van Wees, van Houten et al. at Delft/Philips and Wharam, Pepper et al. at Cambridge. Wharam is not credited here, so the proposed trio is imperfect but workable. I cannot independently verify finer details of who led each group's effort.
assessment.maturity: More than thirty-five years of confirmation and use, so very mature. Possible concern is that recognition is late and several principals are no longer active, which may constrain a laureate set.
uncertainties: Absence of David Wharam from the credited names and the status of living laureates.
Whether the discovery is seen as sufficiently distinct from the quantum Hall prizes already given.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realise Hubbard-type models with tunable parameters, including the superfluid to Mott insulator transition and single-site-resolved quantum gas microscopy. This created a general-purpose analogue quantum simulator and opened a regime in which many-body physics can be observed with microscopic control.
assessment.attribution: Jaksch, Zoller and colleagues proposed the Bose-Hubbard realisation; Greiner and Bloch performed the 2002 Mott transition experiment and later microscopy; Esslinger realised fermionic Mott states; Cirac also appears in the credited names. Choosing three requires dropping Esslinger and Cirac, and Jaksch is not on the list, which makes credit allocation contestable.
assessment.maturity: Widely reproduced across many labs and a mature subject, with ongoing development of quantum simulation of open questions such as the Fermi-Hubbard phase diagram. Timing is reasonable.
uncertainties: Several equally strong contributors, so a three-person cut is arbitrary.
Overlap with the 2001 BEC prize and the 2025 and 2012 AMO-adjacent recognitions.
Scientific payoff for solving open problems such as the Hubbard model at low temperature is still unfolding.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single nitrogen-vacancy centres gave a room-temperature solid-state qubit with long coherence, enabling nanoscale magnetometry, thermometry and biological sensing. It is a striking example of a controllable quantum system in a solid and a bridge between quantum information and sensing.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Jelezko reported the first optical detection of single NV spins in 1997 and coherent control soon after. Lukin contributed theory and key experiments on quantum registers and sensing, and Hanson, Awschalom, Childress and others have strong claims that are not all in this credited list. The core attribution to Wrachtrup and Jelezko is clear; the third slot is debatable.
assessment.maturity: Independently reproduced by many groups and widely used, with commercial sensors emerging. Quantum-sensing claims in biology are still developing, so some applications are not yet mature.
uncertainties: Whether Lukin or other contributors should hold the third position.
Prize-worthiness of sensing applications versus the underlying discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cavity optomechanics brought mechanical resonators into the quantum regime, with ground-state cooling, quantum-limited readout and entanglement of macroscopic mechanical modes with light or microwaves. This extends tests of quantum mechanics to macroscopic objects and relates directly to the macroscopic quantum phenomena recognised in 2025.
assessment.attribution: Cleland's group demonstrated the first quantum ground state of a mechanical resonator (with Martinis' group), Kippenberg developed radiation-pressure cooling and microresonator platforms, and Aspelmeyer contributed quantum-regime experiments and theory. Painter, Teufel, Lehnert and others also made decisive experiments, so the attribution is crowded.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed in several laboratories and platforms, but applications and the final conceptual payoff are still emerging. Recognition might be somewhat early compared with the alternatives.
uncertainties: Crowded credit including Painter, Teufel and Lehnert.
Whether the discovery is a single clean breakthrough or a broad programme.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Programmable arrays of individually trapped Rydberg atoms allow controllable interactions, many-body quantum simulation and emerging gate-based processing with hundreds of qubits. The field is exciting and has produced rapid, vivid demonstrations of new quantum phases.
assessment.attribution: Credited names include five people, and the underlying idea of Rydberg blockade gates came from Jaksch, Cirac, Zoller, Lukin and others, with Saffman, Browaeys, Grangier and Lukin making decisive experiments. Allocation of credit is far from settled.
assessment.maturity: Mature relative to nearly all candidates only in part: the field is very young and rapidly evolving, and independent reproduction at scale is still ongoing. Recognition is likely premature, though it may become a strong candidate.
uncertainties: Premature given rapid ongoing progress.
Complex credit allocation between theory proposals and several experimental groups.
Fault-tolerant performance not yet established.
